Case Study — Healthcare UX

Patient Timeline

2022 – 2025
UX Research Healthcare Figma User Testing Agile
01 — Starting Point

A concept waiting to be tested

When I joined this project, the Patient Timeline existed as an untested concept: give doctors a way to view their patients' history in an intuitive, visual manner.

In preparation for user testing, I created five distinct variations based on this initial idea.

The original concept — static and untested

02 — Design Exploration

Five interaction models

I created five distinct variations to test with clinicians, each representing a different mental model for editing and viewing a timeline.

Variation 1

Form Builder

Step-by-step process where providers specify time range, elements, and styling before viewing the timeline.

Variation 2

Modal Editor

Providers view a default timeline and click elements to open a modal with editing options.

Variations 3 & 4

Panel Editors

Side panels (single or dual) fly out to reveal editing controls while the timeline remains visible.

Variation 5

Tab Editor

Tabs and controls drop down from above the timeline for a compact, keyboard-friendly experience.

03 — Research

User testing

I partnered with a UX researcher to run individual 60-minute remote sessions — 5 physicians, 4 nurse practitioners, and 2 physician assistants — to compare variations and understand unmet needs.

I created the discussion guide, focusing on how much the tool was needed and how well their current EHR tools addressed those needs.

04 — Findings

What we learned

1

Researching medication history in the EHR is time-consuming

"We can't see those scores in an easy workflow. I must dig into the chart to see questions asked, which is silly."

2

All participants wanted to compare medication history with patient data

"I would like the ability to compare patient data and medications. It would make my life easier and be more accurate."

3

EHR integration is critical to adoption

"Any time you put something in a separate app, that creates delays… I'll be more likely to say that's not worth my time."

05 — Prototype Feedback

Design preferences

1

Most preferred the Single Panel or Tab designs

  • Large preview with real-time editing and grouped controls
  • Standardised titles preferred over custom text

"I want to see all options in one area — not all over the screen."

2

Short time intervals are most useful

  • 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years
  • 2-year look-back adequate for most situations

"85% of the time it wouldn't be an issue, but sometimes you do want further than 2 years."

3

Individual medication selection is highly valued

  • Helps with prior authorisations
  • Grouping by condition and alphabetical sort preferred
  • Search box requested by all participants

"I use the search button all the time, every single time. There are patients with so many medications."

06 — Resulting Design

The final direction

Based on the feedback from user testing, I moved forward with a collapsible side panel editor. I prioritised a large timeline view that updates in real-time as the user makes changes.

Within the editor panel, medications are grouped by condition and sorted alphabetically per provider feedback.

Hovering over timeline elements reveals salient information like dates and dosage amounts.

07 — Implementation

Building it for real

I worked closely with developers through agile user stories, handing off specs from Figma. This build was genuinely difficult — I remember memorable calls where I and a developer squinted at math equations trying to get axis markers looking right.

After initial implementation, I iterated on defects and added improvements — including appointment display and a print view.

08 — Launch & Reflection

The End?

In early 2025, the Patient Timeline launched at an ambulatory psychiatric clinic in North Carolina. The medical director was excited for psychiatrists to compare behavioural health surveys with medications over time.

We visited the clinic after launch — the doctors liked the tool, but couldn't use it to compare surveys with medications because they had just switched electronic health records and lost their old survey collection system. Not by choice.

And so, problems that need solving continue to arise...

Case Study — AI / Healthcare UX

Predictive Analytics

2022 – 2025
AI / ML Healthcare Data Visualisation User Testing Figma
01 — Starting Point

Inheriting a project mid-stream

In 2021, a team began developing an ML model to predict a patient's risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD). When I took over design in 2022, one user study had already been completed.

My task: design a pop-out that conveys the model's risk prediction to a primary care doctor in seconds — clearly and credibly.

Design concepts explored in the 2021 user study

02 — Discovery

Getting familiar with the model

I reviewed the 2021 study findings. Four key takeaways shaped my approach:

→

Doctors thought the tool would be useful and would likely prompt earlier referrals to nephrology.

→

Doctors would trust the tool if they could see what's underlying the predictions, or if it had been validated in a study.

→

Many thought it would be useful for both doctor and patient to see which health factors contributed to the model's prediction.

→

Simple visualisations work best for a tool like this.

I also spent several days talking with the PM, tech lead, and a doctor on my team — learning that the model would predict risk of stage 1–2 CKD progressing to stage 3 within up to 5 years, and that contributing factors per patient could be visualised.

Visualisations of contributing factors for two test patients, created by the modelling team

03 — Research

Mockups & user testing

Our teams wanted to display 1-, 2-, and 3-year risk scores. I created several design options for the visualisation, colours, and labelling, then partnered with a UX researcher to test them with primary care doctors.

1

Colour mapping was intuitive

Most expected green, yellow, and red to indicate low, moderate, and high risk.

2

2-year scores weren't useful

1-year, 3-year, and 5-year time frames were all perceived as valuable — 2-year was dropped.

3

Show values, don't hide them

Most liked percentages and values on the contributing factors visualisation. Most also wanted the visualisation visible without expanding a fold.

4

Clinical nuance matters

Some wanted stage 3 CKD to be further split into 3A and 3B.

Text list variation

Bar chart variation

Labelled axis variation

Tree-style design (winner)

User study findings table, colour-coded for pattern analysis

04 — Resulting Design

The winning design

The tree-style visualisation won in testing. Based on feedback, I added percentages to the contributing factors and confirmed with the modelling team whether the prediction covered stage 3A or 3B. I updated time frames from 1-, 2-, 3-year to 1-, 3-, and 5-year.

05 — An Unexpected Turn

Legal implications

Some tools require rigorous testing cycles before they can display a number about a patient. Our legal team determined this was one of those tools — a process that could take years.

In the meantime, my team opted to water down the language. Instead of numbers, the output became "patient requires a closer review or intervention" or "patient does not require a closer review or intervention". We kept the red/green shading to visually differentiate outcomes.

I also created a text-only version of the contributing factors — simpler to build and avoiding any number-based display.

06 — Reflection

In conclusion

Working with predictive analytics has been exciting. The core challenge was turning raw model output into something a doctor could trust and understand in a few seconds.

Next time I get a chance to do something like this, I'll talk to the lawyers a little earlier in the process.

This project was quickly followed by two more risk models by the same team — one for Diabetic Foot Ulcer and one for Hypertensive Crisis Onset. Both were built faster because we reused the design framework established here.
